items.title: Google's Agents CLI gets an Extension System — override or add commands without forking
items.summary: Starting in v1.5.0 (now experimental in v1.8.0), Agents CLI extensions are Git-distributed directories with a manifest that can override built-in commands (like deploy or run) or add new ones — installed from any Git host, pinned to a commit SHA in a lockfile, with project scope beating user scope on conflicts. A first-party LangChain/LangGraph/Deep Agents extension ships too, reimplementing six commands with no google-adk dependency.
items.why: This is a real escape hatch from the usual choice between forking a CLI or living with its defaults — you can wrap deploy with your own security gate or swap in a different framework's lifecycle without touching Google's code.
items.action: If you're on Agents CLI, try the worked example in the post: an sbom-deploy extension that wraps deploy with a syft/grype scan and blocks on critical vulnerabilities.

items.title: Google's Agent Compute Engine gives every agent task its own hardware-isolated microVM
items.summary: Shubham Saboo (Google): traditional VMs boot too slowly and containers share a kernel, so Google built a purpose-made compute layer for Gemini's agents instead. Each task gets its own microVM with its own kernel, its own short-lived credentials (injected outside the microVM, not handled by the agent), and its own disk that persists across sessions — pausing to near-zero cost when the agent is just thinking, resuming from a snapshot when it acts again. Already powers Gemini and Antigravity; coming to Google Cloud in preview in the coming months.
items.why: The design choices here — credentials the agent process never touches, a machine that costs nothing while idle — are the actual answer to how you let an agent run unsupervised without handing it the keys.
items.action: If you're building anything that gives an agent its own sandbox today (a container, a VM, a Daytona/E2B box), compare your credential-handling against this pattern — inject at the edge, never inside the agent's reach.

items.title: Arpit Bhayani fine-tuned a 3B model to replace a 3,500-token incident-triage prompt
items.summary: A holiday experiment, not a production claim: he generated 5,116 synthetic incident-triage conversations from his own simulator, fine-tuned a 3B model with QLoRA (loss-masked so the model learns only its own decisions, not simulated tool output), and tested it on 500 held-out synthetic scenarios. Result: 93.0% success vs. a large hosted model's 92.0% (cached), input tokens per incident down 91.3% (5,200 to 450), cost per 1,000 incidents down 8.4x ($1.85 to $0.22). Tradeoff he's upfront about: change the workflow, retrain the model — a prompt you can just edit.
items.why: It's a clean demonstration that a procedure can live in a small model's weights instead of a big model's prompt — genuinely cheaper, but proven only on his own simulator, not real incidents yet.
items.action: If you have a stable, repetitive agent workflow burning big-model tokens on the same SOP every time, this is a concrete template (data gen, loss masking, QLoRA) for compiling it into a small local model instead.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude just made formal software verification feasible at real scale
items.summary: Working with Theorem, Claude proved no-crash memory-safety properties for 239 entry points across 123 open-source libraries at the compiled RISC-V level — about 180 million lines of Rocq proof, mostly checked automatically rather than reviewed by humans. The process surfaced hundreds of real bugs along the way, including a rediscovered CVE in libexpat, and a PDF-reader pass found in one week roughly as many security bugs as are typically reported in a year.
items.why: Formal verification has always been real but impractical outside tiny codebases; this is the first credible sign it's becoming something you could actually run on your own repo, not just a research demo.
items.action: Theorem is offering to run this same verification pipeline on other open-source projects — worth a look if you maintain anything performance- or memory-safety-sensitive.

items.title: Code Comprehensor: hierarchical documentation + cross-modal retrieval for understanding large repos
items.summary: Accepted at ICSME 2026. Builds a call graph of a codebase, uses code-aware LLMs to write hierarchical documentation across it, then trains a contrastive dual encoder on that documentation so an MCP-based orchestrator can retrieve the right code neighborhood -- not just one function, but its callers, callees, and siblings -- as grounded context for a question. Evaluated on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-line-of-code repo; the full framework's answers score above 90% faithfulness under RAGAS LLM-as-judge.
items.why: This is a direct attempt at giving an LLM the surrounding context a large, fast-changing codebase actually needs, not just the one function it's looking at.
items.action: If you're prototyping retrieval over a large repo for an agent, the three-part structure here (call graph -> hierarchical doc generation -> contrastive retrieval over that documentation) is a concrete architecture to borrow pieces from.

eval.reason: Genuine new paper/architecture; checked against full repo history, no prior coverage found.

items.title: Your Agent Fix Just Broke Something Else -- Sofia Jakovcevic, Arize AI
items.summary: A one-line 'confirm before any action' prompt change made a support agent 17 points safer and 17 points worse at finishing tasks -- net zero, and invisible until someone actually measured both. Walks through a five-step regression loop: build datasets from production traces (not synthetic data), score with evaluators, run baseline experiments, compare changes, then gate merges in CI so a PR can't land without passing the suite.
items.why: The core point is sharp and easy to forget: agents fail at runtime, not in the diff -- a one-line, easy-to-approve code review can hide a large, invisible behavioral shift that only your traces would catch.
